9702-1.1.1.motivate: Two students record the same length as "0.75" and "75". Neither can be judged until we know what was measured and in what. We need a precise statement of what every measurement consists of.

discover.stem: The mass of a stone is measured as $0.35\ \mathrm{kg}$ and then quoted as $350\ \mathrm{g}$. The stone itself is unchanged. What is different between the two records?

options.A: The physical quantity and the unit
options.B: The numerical magnitude and the unit
options.C: The physical quantity and the numerical magnitude
options.D: The physical quantity, the numerical magnitude and the unit

discover.explanation: Mass is still the quantity being measured. Changing to a smaller unit (g instead of kg) means a larger number is needed for the same mass, so the magnitude and the unit both change.

9702-1.1.1.establish:
What we measure is a **physical quantity**: length, mass, time, temperature, current.

- "0.75" alone tells you nothing, but "0.75 m" does. So every record needs a **numerical magnitude** and a **unit**:
$$Q = \text{numerical magnitude} \times \text{unit},\qquad \text{e.g. } v = 12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$
- The **quantity** is what is measured; the **unit** is the agreed size it is measured in. Temperature is a quantity; kelvin is only a unit, so "kelvin" is not a physical quantity.
- The same length is $0.75\ \mathrm{m} = 750\ \mathrm{mm}$. A smaller unit needs a larger number, and the quantity is unchanged. So the unit need not be an SI unit.
- Only **vector** quantities (force, velocity) also need a direction. Mass, time and energy do not.
- In CAIE 9702 MCQs, pure ratios such as strain or efficiency have no unit, so they are not accepted as physical quantities (in wider SI usage they are called dimensionless quantities).
9702-1.1.1.connect: This is the foundation for the whole course: every later quantity, from force to current, is a magnitude and a unit, and 1.2 fixes which units everything else is built from.
9702-1.1.1.note:
- A physical quantity consists of a numerical magnitude and a unit: $Q = \text{number}\times\text{unit}$.
- The quantity is what is measured (temperature, length); the unit is what it is measured in (kelvin, metre). A unit alone is not a physical quantity.
- A record needs a number and a unit; the unit need not be an SI or base unit (0.75 m = 750 mm).
- Only vector quantities have a direction; scalars have magnitude and unit only.
- CAIE 9702 MCQs treat unit-less ratios (efficiency, strain) as not physical quantities (e.g. Nov 2020 P11 Q1); in wider SI usage they are called dimensionless quantities.
9702-1.1.1.self_explain: Explain in your own words why the record "length = 0.75" is incomplete, and why "0.75 m" and "750 mm" are equally good records of the same length.

9702-1.1.2.motivate: Some exam questions give no data and ask for a reasonable estimate. A slip of a power of ten then gives an absurd answer, so we need a method that gets the size right rather than the exact digits.

discover.stem: A box has a volume of $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. Which is the volume of the box in $\mathrm{m^3}$?

9702-1.1.2.establish:
An estimate is judged on its **order of magnitude**, not its exact digits. So build it from values you already know.

1. Break the quantity into known parts. For kinetic energy: $E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2$.
2. Choose **anchor values**: adult about $80\ \mathrm{kg}$; sprinter covers $100\ \mathrm{m}$ in about $10\ \mathrm{s}$, so $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; atom about $10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$ across; water $1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.
3. Convert to SI **before** substituting. Convert the length, then raise to the power: $1\ \mathrm{cm^3} = (10^{-2})^3\ \mathrm{m^3} = 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3}$. Divide $\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ by 3.6.
4. Substitute: $E_k \approx \tfrac12\times80\times10^2 = 4\times10^3\ \mathrm{J}$.
5. Give 1 or 2 significant figures and sense-check the size.
9702-1.1.2.connect: An estimate is still a magnitude with a unit (1.1.1), so converting to SI correctly is what keeps the power of ten right. You will use this in every later topic.
9702-1.1.2.note:
- Estimate: choose familiar anchors, convert to SI, use the equation, give 1 or 2 s.f., check the order of magnitude.
- Anchors: adult about 80 kg; sprinter about $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; walking about $1.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; atom diameter about $10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$; visible light 400 to 700 nm.
- Densities: water $1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$; air about $1.2\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.
- Convert the length, then cube: $1\ \mathrm{cm^3} = 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3}$.
- $\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}} \div 3.6 = \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
9702-1.1.2.self_explain: Explain why we convert every value to SI units before substituting into an equation, and why $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ is $10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3}$ and not $10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^3}$.
